text: If for some reason you wanted to draw everything that exists on the same chart, a good way would be to use the log of mass and size.

All of these will draw a diagonal line, the density of water. Everything to the left is, by definition, denser than water, so it sinks. Here we have things made of stone and metal. Anything to the right will float.

In the same way, you can draw a line for the density of air at one atmosphere on Earth. It separates things heavier than air from things lighter than air. And as the name says, here are the lighter than air aircrafts, balloons and zeppelins.
Most animals though, live in a much narrower band. That's because we are mostly made of water. Some of us are a little denser than others.
The hippo, for example, can't actually swim. It just bounces along the riverbed.

So, Earth lives in a kind of gravitational Goldilocks zone, just enough mass for its temperature to hold on to oxygen and nitrogen, not enough to hold on to hydrogen and helium.

You can see that on the chart, most of these dots stop following the rocky planets on the left and move to the right, where planets are mostly made of gas. Saturn is actually less dense than water, it could float if you could have a pool big enough.

Now objects keep climbing and then suddenly the trend stops. You can't get a planet much bigger than Jupiter. Objects 10 times, even 80 times more massive than Jupiter are still roughly Jupiter sized.
That's because the pressure in their core is so high that electrons get squeezed out of their atoms and it becomes degenerate matter.

And then right about brown dwarfs, there's a huge split. Some objects veer to the right and some veer to the left because now we are no longer talking about the story of ordinary matter. We are talking about life and death of stars.
